question: What remission rate did tisagenlecleucel achieve in children and young adults with relapsed/refractory B-ALL in the ELIANA trial?
reference_answer: In the ELIANA trial, tisagenlecleucel produced an overall remission rate of about 81% within 3 months in infused children and young adults (about 82% in the updated analysis).

children and young adults

question: What response rates were reported for brexucabtagene autoleucel in adults with relapsed/refractory B-ALL?
reference_answer: In ZUMA-3 (phase 2, 55 treated adults), brexucabtagene autoleucel achieved CR/CRi in 71% (CR 56%); a later analysis of 78 adults reported CR/CRi 73% (CR 60%); in phase 1 the overall response rate was 69% (53% CR, 16% CRi).

adult patients

question: What results has obecabtagene autoleucel (obe-cel) shown in adult B-ALL?
reference_answer: In the FELIX trial (pivotal cohort IIA, n=94), obe-cel achieved CR/CRi in about 77% (76.6%); median duration of response 21.2 months; 12-month EFS about 49.5% and OS about 61%. It was approved in late 2024 for adults with relapsed/refractory B-ALL.

adults

question: How often does severe CRS occur after CD19 CAR-T in ALL?
reference_answer: Rates vary widely with the product, grading system and disease burden: reported grade >=3 CRS ranges from roughly 10% to 45% (a systematic review: 10.2%-45%; reviews cite about 8%-43%).

question: How common is neurotoxicity (ICANS) after CAR-T in ALL?
reference_answer: ICANS occurs in roughly 20%-65% of patients (often around 40%); severe (grade >=3) ICANS is less common (about 0%-21% in pediatric studies) and more frequent and severe in adults (about 40% with 13% severe in children/young adults vs about 50% with 50% severe in adults).

question: How do real-world results with tisagenlecleucel compare with the clinical trial results?
reference_answer: Real-world outcomes were similar to or better than ELIANA: the CIBMTR registry (255 patients) reported CR 85.5%, 12-month EFS 52.4% and OS 77.2%; the PRWCC (185 patients) reported 85% CR at day 28, with 37% of responders later relapsing. Real-world patients often had lower disease burden.
must_include: real-world CR around 85% vs about 81% in ELIANA
outcomes broadly comparable

question: What remission rates have CD22-directed CAR-T cells achieved in patients who relapsed after CD19 CAR-T?
reference_answer: CD22 CAR-T cells induce remission in roughly 60%-80% of patients relapsing after CD19 CAR-T (including CD19-negative relapse), but responses are often short-lived because CD22 expression is downregulated.

limited durability due to CD22 downregulation

question: How long do remissions last after CAR-T in pediatric ALL? What is the long-term event-free survival?
reference_answer: In ELIANA, 12-month EFS was about 50% and OS about 76%; relapse-free survival was about 58% at 24 months and 52% at 36 months, with 3-year OS about 63%. Real-world 12-month EFS was about 52%. Roughly half of patients stay in long-term remission.
must_include: 12-month EFS of about 50%

question: Why do some patients relapse with CD19-negative leukemia after CAR-T?
reference_answer: CD19-negative relapse (antigen escape) causes a large share of relapses (about 40%-60%). Mechanisms include CD19 mutations and alternative splicing that remove the CAR epitope (e.g. exon 2), lineage switch to myeloid leukemia (especially KMT2A-rearranged), trogocytosis, and epitope masking.
must_include: CD19 mutation or alternative splicing
lineage switch to myeloid leukemia
at least one other mechanism (trogocytosis or epitope masking)

question: Why do some patients relapse even though their leukemia is still CD19-positive?
reference_answer: CD19-positive relapse mostly reflects loss of CAR-T persistence or function: CAR-T cells disappear early (seen as early B-cell recovery / short B-cell aplasia) or become exhausted/dysfunctional, so the leukemia still has CD19 but no working CAR-T cells remain.
must_include: loss of CAR-T persistence (e.g. early B-cell recovery)
CAR-T exhaustion or dysfunction

question: How do 4-1BB and CD28 costimulatory domains differ in CAR-T cell persistence?
reference_answer: 4-1BB CARs (e.g. tisagenlecleucel, obe-cel) tend to expand more gradually but persist longer, with a memory-like phenotype and less exhaustion; CD28 CARs (e.g. brexucabtagene) expand rapidly with strong early activity but persist for a shorter time and may be more toxic.
must_include: 4-1BB: longer persistence
CD28: faster/stronger early expansion but shorter persistence

question: Why is lymphodepleting chemotherapy given before CAR-T, and which drugs are used?
reference_answer: Lymphodepletion, usually fludarabine plus cyclophosphamide, removes the patient's own lymphocytes (including regulatory T cells), reducing competition for homeostatic cytokines such as IL-7 and IL-15 and improving CAR-T expansion and persistence; adding fludarabine improved expansion, persistence and disease-free survival.
must_include: fludarabine and cyclophosphamide
improves CAR-T expansion/persistence

question: Why is B-cell aplasia monitored after CAR-T, and how is it managed?
reference_answer: CD19 CAR-T cells also kill normal B cells, so B-cell aplasia is nearly universal while the CAR-T cells are active and is used as a marker of functional CAR-T persistence (early B-cell recovery signals loss of CAR-T and higher risk of CD19-positive relapse). It causes hypogammaglobulinemia and infection risk, managed with immunoglobulin replacement (IVIG) and infection prophylaxis.
must_include: marker of CAR-T persistence
hypogammaglobulinemia/infection risk
immunoglobulin replacement

question: How do CAR-T outcomes differ between children and adults with B-ALL?
reference_answer: Children and young adults generally achieve high remission rates (about 80%-90%) with more durable responses; adults also reach high CR rates (about 70%-80%) but have more severe toxicity (CRS, ICANS) and worse long-term outcomes (e.g. ICANS about 40% with 13% severe in children/young adults vs about 50% with 50% severe in adults).
must_include: adults have more severe toxicity
children have more durable outcomes
must_not: applying pediatric results to adults

question: Should patients have a stem cell transplant after achieving remission with CAR-T?
reference_answer: The evidence is mixed and mostly retrospective. Consolidative allo-HSCT may make remissions more durable for selected high-risk patients (e.g. no prior transplant, short CAR-T persistence, CD28 products, persistent MRD), while others stay in remission with CAR-T alone (only about 9% in ELIANA went to transplant; in ZUMA-3 survival was similar with or without allo-HCT). Decisions are individualized.
must_include: evidence is mixed / not settled
may benefit selected high-risk patients
some patients stay in remission without transplant

question: How does CAR-T compare with blinatumomab or inotuzumab for relapsed B-ALL?
reference_answer: Evidence is limited and mostly retrospective. One comparative study found CD19 CAR-T gave higher CR/CRi rates than blinatumomab, especially with high tumor burden, but with more severe toxicity (CRS 42.6% vs 13.3%, more severe cytopenias). Prior blinatumomab/inotuzumab exposure, especially non-response, has been linked to lower CAR-T response rates.
must_include: CAR-T had higher remission but more toxicity in a retrospective comparison
prior blinatumomab exposure may lower CAR-T efficacy
evidence is limited/retrospective

question: What makes CAR-T harder to use in T-cell ALL than in B-ALL?
reference_answer: T-ALL cells share antigens (e.g. CD7, CD5) with normal T cells, including the CAR-T cells themselves. This causes fratricide (CAR-T cells killing each other), risk of long-lasting T-cell aplasia (immunodeficiency), and risk of malignant T cells contaminating the product. Approaches include gene editing (e.g. CD7 knockout) and alternative targets (e.g. CD99).
must_include: shared antigens between malignant and normal/CAR T cells
fratricide
T-cell aplasia or product contamination

question: How is ICANS graded and treated?
reference_answer: ICANS is graded with the ASTCT consensus system using the ICE score (CAPD in young children), level of consciousness, seizures, motor findings and cerebral edema. Treatment is mainly corticosteroids (e.g. dexamethasone) plus supportive care; tocilizumab does not treat isolated ICANS; anakinra may be used for refractory cases.
must_include: ASTCT grading / ICE score
corticosteroids as the main treatment

question: What is CAR-T-associated HLH/MAS, and how is it recognized?
reference_answer: A rare (about 3.5% in one survey) hyperinflammatory syndrome resembling HLH/MAS (IEC-associated HLH), often appearing as CRS resolves, with very high ferritin (often >10,000 ng/mL), coagulopathy/low fibrinogen, high triglycerides, cytopenias, organomegaly and liver dysfunction. Treated with anakinra and corticosteroids, with ruxolitinib or etoposide for refractory cases.
must_include: hyperinflammatory syndrome
very high ferritin
another feature (coagulopathy, cytopenias, or high triglycerides)

question: What causes prolonged low blood counts (cytopenias) after CAR-T, and how are they managed?
reference_answer: Prolonged or biphasic cytopenias are common. Contributors include lymphodepleting chemotherapy, inflammation (CRS cytokines), prior therapies and limited marrow reserve, and marrow disease burden; scores such as CAR-HEMATOTOX (and an ALL-adapted version) help predict risk. Management includes transfusions, G-CSF, thrombopoietin agonists, and CD34+ stem cell boost in severe cases.
must_include: causes (lymphodepletion, inflammation, marrow reserve or disease burden)
management (transfusion/G-CSF; stem cell boost if severe)

question: What is Kymriah approved for in ALL, and for which age group?
reference_answer: Kymriah is tisagenlecleucel. It was approved by the FDA in August 2017 (EMA 2018) for patients up to 25 years old with B-cell precursor ALL that is refractory or in second or later relapse.
must_include: recognizes Kymriah = tisagenlecleucel
patients up to 25 years

question: What doses of tocilizumab have been used to treat CRS after CAR-T?
reference_answer: Tocilizumab is typically given at 8 mg/kg (maximum 800 mg), which may be repeated after 8 hours, for CRS of grade 2 or higher; one review gives 12 mg/kg for children under 30 kg and 8 mg/kg for patients over 30 kg.

question: What CAR-T cell dose was used for brexucabtagene autoleucel in the ZUMA-3 trial?
reference_answer: In ZUMA-3, the recommended phase 2 dose of brexucabtagene autoleucel (KTE-X19) was 1 × 10^6 CAR T cells per kg; phase 1 tested 2 × 10^6, 1 × 10^6 and 0.5 × 10^6 cells per kg.

question: What does MRD-negative remission mean, and how often does CAR-T achieve it in B-ALL?
reference_answer: MRD-negative remission means no leukemia is detectable even with sensitive tests (flow cytometry, PCR or sequencing), usually below about 1 leukemia cell in 10,000 (10^-4, 0.01%). Most CAR-T remissions in B-ALL are MRD-negative: in ELIANA all responders (about 81%-82%) were MRD-negative by flow cytometry, and other studies report MRD-negative CR rates of roughly 67%-88%.

a rate or range (roughly 67%-90%) or that most CAR-T remissions are MRD-negative
must_not: presenting the overall CR rate as the MRD-negative rate
using blinatumomab MRD results (e.g. 97%) as CAR-T results

question: How does disease burden before infusion affect CAR-T response and CRS?
reference_answer: Higher disease burden before infusion (e.g. >=5% marrow blasts) is linked to worse outcomes: less durable remissions and shorter survival (median EFS 10.6 vs about 4 months and OS 20.1 vs about 12 months for low vs high burden in one study) and more relapse. High burden is also linked to more severe CRS and ICANS, although not every study found this association.
must_include: low burden -> better / more durable outcomes (EFS/OS)
high burden -> more severe CRS and/or neurotoxicity
must_not: claiming high burden improves CAR-T outcomes

question: What results have dual-targeting CD19/CD22 CAR-T cells shown in B-ALL?
reference_answer: Dual-targeting CD19/CD22 CAR-T cells (tandem, bicistronic, co-transduced or co-administered/sequential) give high remission rates, often about 86%-100% (e.g. 99% CR in 195 children with 12-month EFS 73.5%; 100% response with 88% MRD-negative CR in 17 adults with a tandem CAR; 86% CR with AUTO3). Durability is not clearly better than single-target CD19 CAR-T: relapses still occur (mostly CD19+/CD22+ or CD19-/CD22+), and limited persistence of the CD22 component is a concern.
must_include: high remission rates (roughly 86%-100%)
relapses still occur / durability not clearly better than CD19 CAR-T
must_not: claiming dual targeting eliminates relapse

question: How do older adults with B-ALL do after CAR-T?
reference_answer: Evidence in older adults is limited. A post hoc analysis of the FELIX trial (obe-cel) found minimal differences in response, EFS and OS between patients <55 and >=55 years (also >=65). In a phase 1 study of 18 adults >=55 years given CD19 CAR-T as consolidation in first remission, all were MRD-negative at day 28, 18-month EFS was 84% and OS 100%, with no grade >=2 CRS or any ICANS and preserved cognition and function.
must_include: evidence is limited / early-phase
outcomes similar by age in FELIX, or the >=55 consolidation study results (18-month EFS 84%)
must_not: using lymphoma data (e.g. a study with median age 74) as ALL results

question: What results have donor-derived or allogeneic (off-the-shelf) CAR-T cells shown in ALL?
reference_answer: Donor-derived CD19 CAR-T cells (made from the transplant donor's T cells, for relapse after allogeneic transplant) achieved CR in about 79%-89% (e.g. 79% of 43 patients, 1-year EFS 43%), with GVHD and CRS as concerns. Off-the-shelf gene-edited allogeneic products such as UCART19 had lower responses (67% CR/CRi in 21 adults; 48% overall response in 25 patients in CALM), depending on CAR-T expansion, and were often followed by allogeneic transplant.
must_include: donor-derived: CR roughly 79%-89%
off-the-shelf (UCART19): lower response, about 48%-67%
GVHD risk
must_not: confusing donor-derived and off-the-shelf products

question: How often does CAR-T manufacturing fail, and how long does it take from collecting cells to infusion?
reference_answer: Manufacturing usually takes about 1-3 weeks (e.g. 7-14 or 9-14 days; 8-12 days for tisagenlecleucel), and vein-to-vein time (collection to infusion) is about 3-4 weeks or longer (median 20-33 days in some studies; rapid platforms about 9-14 days). In ELIANA, 7 of 88 enrolled patients (about 8%) could not be treated because of manufacturing failure; in large trials 20%-30% of enrolled patients were never infused because of manufacturing failure and/or disease progression or death while waiting.
must_include: manufacturing about 1-3 weeks or vein-to-vein about 3-4 weeks
failure figure: about 8% (7 of 88) in ELIANA, or 20%-30% never infused (failure or progression)
must_not: presenting the 20%-30% not-infused figure as manufacturing failure alone

question: How does a CAR-T cell recognize and kill a leukemia cell?
reference_answer: A CAR is a synthetic receptor. Its outside part, usually an antibody-derived single-chain variable fragment (scFv), binds a surface antigen such as CD19 directly, without needing MHC/HLA presentation. It is linked through a hinge and transmembrane domain to signaling domains inside the cell: CD3-zeta plus a costimulatory domain (4-1BB or CD28). Binding activates the T cell to multiply, release cytokines and release cytotoxic molecules that kill the leukemia cell.
must_include: scFv / antibody-derived part binds CD19 without MHC restriction
CD3-zeta (+ costimulatory) signaling activates the T cell to kill

question: What is lineage switch, and why can leukemia turn myeloid after CAR-T?
reference_answer: Lineage switch is when B-ALL relapses as a myeloid leukemia (e.g. AML): not just loss of CD19 but a change of cell identity (loss of B-cell transcription factors such as PAX5/EBF1, gain of myeloid ones). It reflects leukemia plasticity under sustained CD19-directed immune pressure and is strongly linked to KMT2A (MLL) rearrangement and infant ALL. Among 420 children/young adults given CD19 CAR-T, 12 of 166 relapses (7.2%) were lineage switches, and 9 of those 12 had KMT2A rearrangement.
must_include: relapse as myeloid leukemia (change of lineage, not only CD19 loss)
KMT2A/MLL rearrangement as the main risk factor

question: Why does prior blinatumomab treatment matter for later CAR-T response?
reference_answer: Blinatumomab also targets CD19. Non-response to prior blinatumomab is associated with lower CR rates, shorter relapse-free survival and more CD19-negative relapse after CD19 CAR-T. Mere exposure matters less clearly: one analysis found numerically lower CR/CRi (60% vs 80%) without an effect on RFS or OS. The evidence is retrospective.
must_include: non-response to prior blinatumomab linked to lower CR / worse outcomes
link with CD19-negative relapse or the shared CD19 target
evidence is retrospective or mixed (exposure alone less clearly harmful)

question: How does T-cell exhaustion or poor T-cell fitness affect CAR-T results?
reference_answer: CAR-T products rich in less-differentiated T cells (naive, stem-cell memory, central memory) expand and persist better and are associated with good responses; heavily pretreated patients have fewer such cells. Exhausted or dysfunctional CAR-T cells (from chronic stimulation, tonic signaling or high tumor burden) persist poorly, which leads to early loss of B-cell aplasia and CD19-positive relapse; 4-1BB constructs show less exhaustion than CD28.
must_include: naive/memory (less differentiated) T cells -> better expansion, persistence or response
exhaustion -> poor persistence and relapse

question: Why are humanized CD19 CARs used after a murine CAR-T has failed?
reference_answer: Most CARs use a mouse-derived scFv (e.g. FMC63). The patient's immune system can recognize it as foreign (antibody or T-cell responses) and reject the CAR-T cells, shortening persistence, especially when they are given again. Humanized scFv CARs (e.g. huCART19) aim to avoid this. In a pilot trial of 74 children/young adults, response was 98% in CAR-naive patients and 64% in patients retreated after a prior CAR-T.
must_include: immune rejection of the mouse-derived scFv
about 64% response after prior CAR-T

question: What role does bridging therapy play while CAR-T cells are being made?
reference_answer: Bridging therapy is given between cell collection and infusion to control the leukemia while the product is made, aiming for lower disease burden (ideally remission) at infusion, which improves outcomes and reduces toxicity. Options include chemotherapy (often low-intensity), inotuzumab or blinatumomab. Evidence is mixed: patients who respond to bridging do better, but more intensive bridging (e.g. 2 or more cycles) was linked to lower OS and more severe infections, one large dataset associated bridging with inferior survival, and it can add to cytopenias.
must_include: purpose: control disease / reduce burden while cells are manufactured
tradeoff or mixed evidence (infections, cytopenias, intensity)
must_not: confusing it with bridging to transplant after CAR-T

question: Can CAR-T treat leukemia that has spread to the central nervous system?
reference_answer: Yes. CAR-T cells reach the CNS and CD19 CAR-T can clear CNS leukemia. In 48 patients with CNS leukemia, CNS remission was 85.4% (marrow response 87.5%), and CNS relapse was less common than marrow relapse; real-world data (PRWCC) showed CR in 88% of patients with CNS disease with survival similar to those without. Neurotoxicity is the main concern (grade 3-4 in 22.9%, linked to higher CNS burden), and active symptomatic CNS disease is often excluded from trials.
must_include: CAR-T can clear CNS disease (response roughly 85%-88%)
neurotoxicity concern

question: Do steroids given for side effects reduce how well CAR-T works?
reference_answer: Mostly no. Early concern that steroids blunt CAR-T expansion led to cautious use, but more recent studies found that short-term or early steroids (and tocilizumab) do not significantly reduce CAR-T expansion, efficacy or survival. Some caution remains (reduced expansion in a few patients; prolonged or high cumulative doses are less studied).
must_include: recent evidence: short-term/early steroids do not significantly reduce efficacy
earlier concern or remaining caution

question: Can CAR-T be used in Philadelphia chromosome-positive ALL?
reference_answer: Yes. CAR-T is used in relapsed/refractory Ph-positive ALL (complete molecular remission about 68%; one study reported CR 92.3% in BCR-ABL+ ALL) and is being tested frontline with tyrosine kinase inhibitors: in a phase 2 trial of dasatinib plus sequential CD19/CD22 CAR-T in 28 newly diagnosed adults, complete molecular remission was 85% after CD19 CAR-T and 2-year OS and leukemia-free survival were 92%, with only grade 1 CRS. The evidence is early and single-center.
must_include: CAR-T is effective in Ph+ ALL (high remission rates)
combination with a TKI such as dasatinib (frontline trial: ~85% molecular remission or 92% 2-year OS)
must_not: claiming Ph+ patients cannot receive CAR-T

question: Can patients receive a second CAR-T infusion if the first one fails?
reference_answer: Yes, but responses are lower and often less durable. Retreatment with the same CAR-T gave CR in 40% or fewer in some reports; in a review of 81 reinfusions of 4-1BB CD19 CAR-T, 52% of reinfusions given to prevent relapse achieved CR (38% for B-cell recovery, 78% for hematogones), and lymphodepletion helped. Switching to a humanized CAR after a murine one gave a 64% response. Immune responses against the CAR can cause rejection.
must_include: reinfusion is possible but responses are lower / less durable
a supporting figure (e.g. 52% CR, <=40% CR, or 64% with a humanized CAR)

question: How is CRS graded?
reference_answer: CRS is graded with the ASTCT consensus system (2018) using three signs: fever, hypotension and hypoxia. Grade 1: fever only; grade 2: fever with hypotension not needing vasopressors and/or low-flow oxygen (<=6 L/min); grade 3: a vasopressor and/or high-flow oxygen (>6 L/min); grade 4: multiple vasopressors and/or positive-pressure ventilation or intubation.
must_include: ASTCT consensus grading
based on fever, hypotension and hypoxia, graded by the support needed

question: Which drugs are used for CRS that doesn't respond to tocilizumab?
reference_answer: Corticosteroids (dexamethasone or methylprednisolone, with high doses for life-threatening CRS) are the main next step when CRS does not respond to tocilizumab. Other second-line options, still under investigation, include anakinra (IL-1 receptor antagonist), siltuximab (IL-6 blocker) and, in case reports, etanercept (TNF-alpha inhibitor).
must_include: corticosteroids
anakinra or siltuximab

question: Which lab markers (IL-6, ferritin, CRP) are linked to severe CRS?
reference_answer: High IL-6, IFN-gamma, IL-8, IL-10, IL-15, MCP-1, CRP and ferritin have been associated with severe CRS. In one study CRP above about 20 mg/dL predicted severe CRS (sensitivity 86%, specificity 100%); in another, higher peak CAR copies and IL-6 were independent risk factors. CRP and ferritin are nonspecific (often raised by the cancer itself), so prediction is imperfect; very high ferritin (>10,000 ng/mL) suggests CAR-associated HLH.
must_include: IL-6, CRP and ferritin (and other cytokines) associated with severe CRS
markers are imperfect/nonspecific, or the CRP >20 mg/dL example

question: What infections happen after CAR-T, and when?
reference_answer: Infections are common after CAR-T and the leading cause of non-relapse mortality. Most are bacterial and occur early (first about 30 days), related to neutropenia and lymphodepleting chemotherapy; later infections are more often viral or opportunistic, linked to prolonged cytopenias, B-cell aplasia and hypogammaglobulinemia. Antiviral and Pneumocystis prophylaxis and immunoglobulin replacement are used.
must_include: early infections mostly bacterial (first ~30 days)
later infections more viral/opportunistic

question: What long-term effects are seen years after CAR-T?
reference_answer: Long-term effects include persistent B-cell aplasia with hypogammaglobulinemia (ELIANA: persistent B-cell aplasia in 71% at 12 months and 59% at 24 months) causing infection risk and needing immunoglobulin replacement; prolonged cytopenias; rare secondary malignancies (1.7% in 420 children, most with prior transplant or radiation); and possible growth effects. Neurocognitive, fertility and psychosocial effects are still being studied; long-term data are limited.
must_include: B-cell aplasia / hypogammaglobulinemia with infection risk
secondary malignancies (rare)
long-term data are limited / still being studied

must_not: inventing a cure rate or phase 3 result

question: What long-term (5-year) survival has been reported after CAR-T for B-ALL?
reference_answer: Long-term data come mainly from ELIANA (tisagenlecleucel, children and young adults): with more than 5 years of follow-up, 5-year OS was about 55% and 5-year EFS about 36%-42% (sources report different EFS values), and most relapses happened in the first 18 months. Selected settings report higher figures (e.g. 5-year OS 75% / EFS 50% with sequential CD19/CD22 CAR-T after transplant relapse; 5-year EFS about 62% when CD28-based CAR-T was followed by transplant).
must_include: ELIANA 5-year OS about 55%
5-year EFS roughly 36%-42%, or that sources differ
must_not: using chemotherapy-era survival (e.g. 5-year OS >90%) as CAR-T results

question: How often do patients relapse within the first year after CAR-T?
reference_answer: Relapse is common early: reviews state nearly 50% of patients relapse within 1 year; in ELIANA 12-month EFS was about 50% and most relapses occurred within the first 18 months; about 60% of responders are alive and disease-free at 1 year. In a 420-patient study, 39.5% relapsed overall.
must_include: roughly 40%-50% relapse within the first year (or 12-month EFS about 50%)
most relapses happen early (first 12-18 months)

question: What share of patients in CAR-T trials go on to a stem cell transplant afterwards?
reference_answer: It varies widely by product and center: in ELIANA only about 9%-15% (10 of 65 responders) went on to transplant; in ZUMA-3 20% (11 of 55); in the NIH CD28-based pediatric trial about 75% of patients in MRD-negative CR proceeded to transplant.
must_include: varies widely between trials
at least two figures, e.g. ELIANA ~9%-15%, ZUMA-3 ~20%, NIH ~75%

question: How common is CD19-negative relapse compared with CD19-positive relapse?
reference_answer: In 420 children and young adults given CD19 CAR-T, 39.5% relapsed; of the relapses about 50% were CD19-positive, 41% CD19-negative and 7.2% lineage switch. CD19-negative relapse has worse outcomes (12-month OS 30% vs 68% after CD19-positive relapse).
must_include: about half of relapses CD19-positive and about 40% CD19-negative

question: How often does CAR-T fail to produce any remission at all?
reference_answer: About 10%-20% of patients have primary resistance to CD19 CAR-T and never reach remission, consistent with remission rates of roughly 80%-90% in pivotal studies (e.g. 82% in ELIANA). Off-the-shelf products fail more often (52% nonresponders with UCART19).
must_include: about 10%-20% primary resistance / no remission

question: How soon after infusion does CRS usually start?
reference_answer: CRS usually starts within the first few days: median onset about 3 days for tisagenlecleucel, 4-5 days in other studies, usually within about 6 days. ICANS typically comes later (about 7-10 days).
must_include: usually within the first days (median about 3-5 days)
must_not: giving ICANS timing as CRS timing

question: How common is CRS of any grade after CD19 CAR-T in ALL?
reference_answer: CRS of any grade is very common: about 77% in ELIANA (tisagenlecleucel) and 89% in an adult trial, so most patients develop some CRS; severe CRS is less common and varies by product and disease burden.
must_include: most patients (roughly 70%-90%) develop some CRS
must_not: giving only the severe-CRS rate as the overall rate

question: How many patients die from treatment-related causes (not leukemia) after CAR-T?
reference_answer: Treatment-related deaths are uncommon: a meta-analysis estimated treatment-related death at about 1%. Deaths that occur are mainly from infections (the leading cause of non-relapse mortality), severe CRS, or rarely neurotoxicity (e.g. brain herniation). Non-relapse mortality is much higher when CAR-T is followed by a second transplant (3-year NRM about 41% in one study).
must_include: uncommon, about 1% in a meta-analysis
infections (or CRS/neurotoxicity) as causes

question: What results have been reported for CAR-T in infants with ALL?
reference_answer: Data are small and retrospective but encouraging: in 14 infants given tisagenlecleucel, 64% reached MRD-negative remission and 50% stayed in remission at last follow-up, with few severe toxicities; a European study of 35 children/infants under 3 reported 86% MRD-negative CR and 14% severe CRS. Concerns include KMT2A rearrangement, lineage switch and difficult leukapheresis.
must_include: data are small/retrospective
about 64% MRD-negative remission in 14 infants, or 86% in children under 3

question: Why do CAR-T cells multiply inside the patient's body after infusion?
reference_answer: When the CAR binds its target (CD19) on leukemia cells and normal B cells, CAR signaling activates the T cell and it proliferates inside the body, so CAR-T is a 'living drug'. Lymphodepleting chemotherapy helps by removing competing lymphocytes so cytokines such as IL-7 and IL-15 support expansion; expansion peaks around 1-2 weeks, and more antigen (higher disease burden) is linked to greater expansion.
must_include: binding the target (CD19) activates the CAR-T cells to proliferate
lymphodepletion or the amount of antigen supports expansion

question: What is trogocytosis, and why does it matter for CAR-T?
reference_answer: Trogocytosis is the transfer of membrane proteins between cells in contact: CAR-T cells pull CD19 off leukemia cells. This lowers CD19 on the leukemia (reversible antigen loss that helps escape) and puts CD19 on CAR-T cells, which are then killed by other CAR-T cells (fratricide). Lower-affinity CARs reduce it.
must_include: transfer of CD19 from leukemia cells to CAR-T cells
antigen loss/escape and fratricide

question: How can leukemia cells end up inside a CAR-T product, and what can happen?
reference_answer: If leukemia cells are collected with the T cells and survive manufacturing, one can accidentally receive the CAR gene. The CAR on that leukemia cell binds its own CD19, masking it from CAR-T cells and flow cytometry, which causes an apparently CD19-negative, resistant relapse. It is rare; purifying T cells in the starting material prevents it.
must_include: leukemia cell accidentally transduced with the CAR during manufacturing
the CAR masks CD19 so the leukemia escapes (relapse)

question: What causes cytokine release syndrome in the body?
reference_answer: When CAR-T cells engage CD19 they activate and release cytokines (e.g. IFN-gamma), which activate bystander immune cells, especially monocytes and macrophages. These release large amounts of IL-6 and IL-1 (and IL-10, GM-CSF), creating a body-wide inflammatory cascade that causes fever, low blood pressure and low oxygen.
must_include: CAR-T activation triggers a cytokine cascade
monocytes/macrophages releasing IL-6 and/or IL-1

question: Why does tocilizumab work for CRS but not for ICANS?
reference_answer: CRS is driven by IL-6 in the blood, so blocking the IL-6 receptor with tocilizumab works. Tocilizumab does not cross the blood-brain barrier, so it does not treat the brain inflammation of ICANS; blocking the receptor also briefly raises serum IL-6, which may leak into the CSF and worsen ICANS. ICANS is treated mainly with corticosteroids.
must_include: tocilizumab does not cross the blood-brain barrier
IL-6 rise after receptor blockade may worsen ICANS, or steroids are used for ICANS

question: How do low CD19 or CD22 levels on leukemia cells affect CAR-T response?
reference_answer: Lower antigen levels make leukemia cells harder for CAR-T cells to kill: relapse after CD22 CAR-T is linked to reduced CD22 site density (without mutations), and low antigen density reduces killing. For CD19 the evidence is mixed: a study of 166 patients found CD19-dim leukemia responded as well to tisagenlecleucel as CD19-normal leukemia. Dual targeting is one approach.
must_include: reduced CD22 density linked to relapse after CD22 CAR-T, or low density reduces killing
evidence mixed for CD19 (CD19-dim responded as well in one large study)

question: How are CAR-T cells made from a patient's blood?
reference_answer: 1) Leukapheresis collects the patient's T cells; 2) T cells are enriched and activated (e.g. with anti-CD3/CD28 beads); 3) the CAR gene is introduced, usually with a lentiviral or retroviral vector (sometimes non-viral); 4) cells are expanded with cytokines (IL-2 or IL-7/IL-15) to the needed dose; 5) they are quality-tested, often cryopreserved, and infused after lymphodepletion.
must_include: leukapheresis collects the patient's T cells
genetic modification (usually a viral vector) and expansion before infusion
